Najd Rebellion was a series of armed conflicts and uprisings that took place in Najd after the collapse of the Emirate of Diriyah after its defeat by Ottoman forces. The revolution represented resistance against the Ottoman Caliphate and internal power struggles, as some local rulers sought to preserve the Ottoman Caliphate while others fought for independence. The movement was eventually led by Turki bin Abdullah Al Saud, the grandson of Mohammed bin Saud, the founder of the First Saudi state.
Background
After the Wahhabi expansion of Hejaz, the Wahhabi war began, leading to the defeat of Saudi forces and the subsequent seizure of their capital Diriyah by Ibrahim Pasha, son of Muhammad Ali Pasha. Members of the Al Saud family were forced to flee and hide themselves from the pursuit of the Ottoman forces. After the siege of Diriyah, Ibrahim Pasha founded regional princes for the Najd administration, although these appointments led to internal conflicts as different factions competed for hegemony.
Rebellion
The rise of Ibn Muammar
Ibrahim Pasha left Najd in a state of ruin and suffering from famine before returning to Egypt. After his departure, Mohammed bin Mishary bin Muammar traveled from Al-Ayina to the destroyed city of Diriyah and began to rebuild it. Many former residents who fled during Ibrahim Pasha's campaign returned, and Ibn Muammar established Diriyah as the capital of his emirate. His territory expanded to include Al-Kharj, Riyadh, Harimala and Al-Tashm.
Ibn Muammar ruled many of Najd under Ottoman sovereignty until the emergence of Mishary bin Saud Al Saud, the brother of Abdullah bin Saud. After escaping from captivity near Yanbu, Mishary hid in tattoos, gathered Al Saud loyalists from Qassim and Al-Zulfi, and walked in Diriyah. Although Ibn Muammar initially swore allegiance, he later reconsidered and mobilized forces in Sados with the support of Hermila's commanders. With the additional support of the leader of the Mutayr tribe, Faisal bin Taban Al-Duwish, Ibn Muammar captured Diriyah and imprisoned Mishari bin Saud in Sadus.
After the arrest of Mishari, Ibn Muammar advanced to Riyadh where Turki bin Abdullah took refuge. Turki fled to Al-Hayer in the south of Najd, which prompted Ibn Muammar to appoint his son Mishari as governor of Riyadh. Meanwhile, Muhammad Ali Pasha sent a 400-strong force under Bush Agha to capture Mishari. Learning the presence of Turki bin Abdullah in Druma, Ibn Muammar sent his son with 100 soldiers, but Turki defeated them and captured them. Turki then took control of Diriyah and Riyadh, and Ibn Muammar was arrested, and when Mikhail's death was confirmed in captivity, both Ibn Muammar and his son were executed.
Siege of Riyadh
Faisal bin Taban Al-Duwish and Ghobush Agha tried to besiege Imam Turki bin Abdullah in Riyadh. Turki's forces successfully resisted, forcing the siege to abandon it. In response, Muhammad Ali Pasha ordered all Ottoman forces in Medina to march to Riyadh under the command of Hussein Bey. The Ottoman queue arrived in Riyadh without opposition and surrounded a Turk in the royal palace. Under the darkness, Turki and his supporters fled to Al-Hilweh in the south of Najd. The remaining defenders surrendered, as Hussein Bey executed 70 Turkish supporters and captured Omar bin Abdul Aziz with his son Abdul Malik.
Hassan Bey's arrival and the failed campaigns
After Hussein Bey's withdrawal, the Sharif of Medina Hassan Pasha sent a 800-strong cavalry force led by Hassan Bey (Abu Zaher). This unit destroyed Oniza, Jebel Shammar, Al-Majmaah and Sudair, while attempts to collect zakat from the Bedouins sparked widespread opposition throughout Najd.
Battle of Al-Hayer
Months later, Ottoman forces from Riyadh and Manfouha led by Ibrahim Kashif (brother of Musa Kashif), accompanied by local princes Nasser bin Nasser Al-Aidi, the Emir of Riyadh, Al-Kharj, and Musa bin Mazrou, the Emir of Manfouha, attacked the tribe of Sabaa in Al-Bida, south of Riyadh. Suba', led by Sheikh Mohammed bin Daghim Al-Omani Al-Subaie, was able to defeat the Ottomans and those with them, killing more than 300 soldiers including Ibrahim Kashf and Nasser Al-Aidi and the escape of Musa bin Mazrou.
Battle of Majzal
The Ottoman garrison in Al-Majmaah, led by Musa Kashif, attacked the nearby Sahl tribe but suffered defeat with more than 30 soldiers killed, including Kashif. The survivors retreated to Al-Majmaah alongside Oniza Amir Abdullah Al-Jami.
Oniza Revolution
Residents of Oniza revolted against the 600-strong Ottoman garrison led by Muhammad Agha, in protest against repressive taxes and misconduct. After the forces were besieged in Al-Safa Palace and nearly seventy soldiers were killed, a peace agreement allowed the Ottomans to withdraw, and only the Riyadh garrison remained in Najd.
Return of Turki
The first attack on Riyadh
During the month of Ramadan 1823, Turki bin Abdullah returned with 30 men, and received support from the leaders of the Muham, the Calval and Al-Sudair, and established a race as his base. His attack on the Ottoman garrisons of 600 soldiers in Riyadh and Manfouha failed, forcing him to retreat to Erka where he repelled an Ottoman counterattack.
Subjugation of Najd
In late 1823, a Turk advanced from Erka to seize Derma and kill her prince. As the conflict split in Najd, Turki defeated opposition leaders including Majid bin Ahmed from Al-Majma'ah and Hamad bin Mubarak from Harimalat. The rulers of Al-Zulfi, Ghat, Munich, Sudair and Shaqra surrendered without resistance. Manfouha surrendered after negotiations with Prince Ibrahim bin Salama, who expelled the Ottoman garrison to join Riyadh forces.
Expedition of Riyadh (1824)
By August 1824, Turk had mobilized all the troops from Manfuha to besiege Riyadh. After initial clashes forced Ottoman forces into the city, a month-long siege followed. Turki temporarily withdrew when Faisal al-Dawish reinforced the Ottomans, but resumed the attack after Davis left. The commander of the garrison Abu Ali Al-Maghrabi negotiated a safe corridor before surrendering, in the Ottoman withdrawal from Najd.
Consequences
While the Ottoman Empire focused on the Greek War of Independence, Turki expanded its authority through campaigns in Al-Kharj, Qassim and Jabal Shammar. By 1828, each Najd recognized his rule. After his son Faisal escaped from Egyptian captivity, Turki sent him against the Emirate of Bani Khaled. The subsequent battle of Al-Sabiya witnessed the defeat of Faisal's forces from the tribes of Qahtan, Ajman and Sabia for Prince Majid bin Arir (allied with Anizah and Mutayr). Majid's death hastened Al Saud's invasion of Al-Ahsa and Qatif.
